title: Clinical AI Interpretation: Limits and Escalation
summary: AI interpretation failure modes can harm patients. Learn dialect risks, negation errors, and escalation best practices. August 2026.
body_markdown:
###


Accuracy varies by language and dialect, so a blended accuracy number from a vendor tells you almost nothing useful. See our validation study for accuracy figures by language. Performance across any AI system tracks the volume of clinical training data available for each language. High-resource languages like Spanish and Mandarin perform better; thinly represented dialects and low-resource languages carry higher error risk. Ask vendors for accuracy figures broken out by specific language and dialect, not a single aggregate score.


###


Any tool processing a clinical conversation is handling protected health information and must operate under a signed Business Associate Agreement with your organization. Beyond the BAA, confirm that the vendor encrypts data in transit and at rest, strips patient identifiers on-device before any cloud transmission, defines how long transcripts are retained, and de-identifies data used in quality-review workflows. Consumer translation apps do not meet these requirements; if a vendor cannot answer these questions plainly, that gap is your liability.


###


Mapping the full continuum matters because a well-interpreted visit still fails if follow-up call summaries or prescription labels go out in a language the patient cannot read.


###


The failure modes that carry the most clinical risk are negation errors, numeral mistakes, omissions, and hallucinations. A negation error turns "no known allergies" into an allergy confirmation, sending care in the wrong direction. A numeral error turns 15 milligrams into 50. An omission drops a reported symptom entirely. A hallucination adds clinical detail the patient never said. All of them present as fluent speech, so no one in the room hears the error land. Quality-control systems designed to catch these specific error types are the mechanism that makes AI interpretation safe to deploy at scale.


###


The 2024 final rule implementing Section 1557 requires that patients with limited English proficiency can understand and participate in their care; the rule permits machine translation and does not mandate human interpreters for specific encounter types. Accountability stays with your organization regardless of which tools you deploy. Your organization owns the quality standard, the escalation policy, and the outcome. That means a written language-access policy, defined escalation rules, audit logging, staff training, and a process for reporting near-misses all belong to you, not your vendor.
